## Welcome

- Experiments are one of the main ways we expand our understanding of biology
- This course: **design** experiments well, **analyze** the data in R, **communicate** the results
- Three modules: R Crash Course → Data Exploration → Statistical Analysis and Interpretation

## A question to sit with

> If you ran the same experiment twice, would you trust the second result as much as the first?

- A good design makes the answer "yes"
- A bad design can make even a huge effect impossible to trust

## Why design comes before analysis

- No statistical test can fix a poorly designed study
- Common failure modes we'll dissect this semester:
  - Pseudoreplication (measuring the same unit many times, treating it as many replicates)
  - Confounding (treatment tangled up with some other variable)
  - Underpowered studies (too few replicates to detect a real effect)

## A biology example

- Question: does a fertilizer increase plant growth?
- Naive approach: one plant, control side vs. treated side, measured many times
- Problem: **n = 1 plant** — no replication of the actual experimental unit
- We'll spend Weeks 5–6 building the vocabulary to catch this

## What "medium complexity" looks like by the end

- Import and clean real data
- Visualize it honestly
- Choose a design and a matching statistical test
- Fit that model in R, check its assumptions, interpret the result
